newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian cyclones leave trail of death, destruction.
newsitem.headline: Indian cyclones leave trail of death, destruction.

text.p: Thousands of people have been killed in about 70 cyclones that have raked the low-lying coast of India's Andhra Pradesh state in the past century, meteorological records show.

The latest cyclone that tore across the southeastern state on Wednesday killed more than 500 people, left thousands homeless, capsized ships, disrupted power and telephone lines and wreaked havoc in the rice-growing Godavari districts, officials said.
In June this year, a cyclone killed more than 120 people and damaged crops worth 42.4 million rupees ($1.2 million) across some 3,668 hectares (9,064 acres).
A minor cyclone last month disrupted rail traffic but did not cause much damage.

In a cyclone, winds blow spirally inwards towards a centre of low barometric pressure. Called a cyclone in the Indian Ocean and Australia, the same storm is designated a typhoon in the China Sea and West Pacific and a hurricane in the Caribbean Sea and Atlantic Ocean.
Andhra Pradesh is the most vulnerable of all Indian states to cyclones and to flooding because of its flat coast.

More than 10,000 people died in November 1977 when a cyclone with winds of more than 200 km (125 miles) an hour set off 15-metre (50-foot) high tidal waves that submerged Machilipatnam town and swept 12 km (eight miles) inland.
The 1977 storm caused damage in 830 villages, affecting 5.4 million people. It also damaged 1.4 million hectares (3.5 million acres) of cropland.

In May 1990, a cyclone with wind speeds of 220 to 250 km (140 to 160 miles) an hour struck the coast. But authorities had evacuated 650,000 people inland to safety, and many more rushed to the 500-odd shelters that were built after the 1977 cyclone.
The death toll was 967 from the 1990 storm, which destroyed or damaged 1.6 million homes, causing more than 22 billion rupees ($650 million) worth of destruction.

The government has now set up an early warning system to aid local officials. When a storm approaches, the meteorological department issues bulletins by radio to local police. State television and radio issue warnings at frequent intervals.
